Mir Shahe Alam: Govt unaware of EC’s UP election date announcement
item.description:
State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam has said the government has no knowledge of the Election Commission’s plan to hold Union Parishad (UP) elections in seven phases.
He made the remarks while speaking to journalists at the Secretariat on Tuesday morning, a day after Election Commissioner Abul Fazl Md Sanauallah announced the tentative schedule for the elections. “The government knows nothing about the announcement of the UP election dates. The Local Government Ministry is also unaware of it,” the state minister said.
He said there had been no correspondence between the government and the Election Commission regarding the election schedule, nor had there been any discussion through other channels.
“The Election Commission is an independent body and has the constitutional authority to conduct elections,” Mir Shahe Alam said.
He added that, under the usual practice, the EC discusses local government elections with the government before announcing the schedule. Preparatory meetings and law and order committee meetings are also held, involving issues such as the budget.
“But no such discussion has taken place between the Election Commission and the government or the Local Government Ministry,” he said.
On Monday, Election Commissioner Abul Fazl Md Sanauallah said the UP elections would be held in seven phases, with the first phase tentatively scheduled for November 12.
Speaking to journalists at the Election Commission building in Agargaon, he said the first phase would mark the beginning of the local government elections.
The tentative dates for the subsequent phases are December 13, December 30, January 17, February 4, April 22 and May 27.
The EC had earlier planned to announce the election schedule in August and begin local government elections in October.
In June, the then local government minister told Parliament that local government elections could begin across the country in phases from September or October after the monsoon season. However, the plan did not materialise.

item.title: Century-old floating vegetable market brings relief to Bagerhat farmers
item.description:
A century-old floating vegetable market in Gajalia Union of Kachua upazila in Bagerhat has become a major trading hub for farmers, with vegetables worth around Tk20-25 lakh sold in just four hours on each market day.
The market, held every Sunday and Wednesday on the Gajalia Canal, sees seasonal transactions of nearly Tk4 crore.
Rows of boats loaded with fresh cucumbers, bottle gourds, bitter gourds, ash gourds, pumpkins, ridge gourds and yardlong beans gather on the canal from early morning. Farmers sell their produce directly to wholesalers, who come from Bagerhat and neighbouring districts.
Wholesalers from Barisal, Pirojpur, Jhalakathi, Barguna and Chandpur also visit the market by boats and trawlers to purchase vegetables in bulk.
The floating market continues to preserve a traditional form of river-based commerce that was once common across rural Bangladesh.
Local traders said farmers from surrounding villages bring their produce by boat soon after dawn. They anchor along the canal and begin trading, with the number of boats increasing as the morning progresses.
By mid-morning, rows of boats stretch across the canal, with farmers and traders conducting transactions directly from the vessels.
Farmers said selling directly to wholesalers allows them to secure better prices and sell their produce quickly, reducing the risk of spoilage.
Salam Haladar, a trader from Pirojpur, said the market offers a wide range of fresh vegetables in one place.
“We can buy vegetables directly from farmers and collect large quantities at the same time. We then take them to markets in Pirojpur and other areas,” he said.
Sultan Sheikh, a trader from Barishal, said the regular presence of farmers makes it possible to purchase large quantities within a short period.
“Trading starts early in the morning and large transactions are completed within a few hours. If communication facilities improve, the volume of business could increase significantly,” he said.
Local residents said the market has been operating on the Gajalia Canal for more than 100 years. Generations of farmers have relied on it to sell vegetables grown on their land.
Rajjak Molla, a local farmer, said he brings vegetables to the market by boat on market days.
“Wholesalers buy directly from us, so our produce is sold quickly and transportation costs are relatively low. Without this market, we would have to travel to distant markets, which would cause us much more trouble,” he said.
However, poor infrastructure remains a major challenge for the market.
The road leading to the market is in poor condition, while there are no designated facilities for boats and trawlers to anchor. Farmers and traders face additional difficulties during the monsoon.
Abdullah Al Mamun, a local resident, said the market could expand significantly if basic infrastructure were improved.
“There is no proper arrangement for anchoring boats and trawlers. The road is also in poor condition. Facilities for loading and unloading goods and better market management could increase trading several times,” he said.
Mohammad Motahar Hossain, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Bagerhat, said the floating market plays an important role in the local agricultural economy.
“Farmers can quickly sell their produce to wholesalers, while consumers in different areas get fresh vegetables without much delay,” he said.
He acknowledged the market's infrastructural shortcomings and said steps would be taken to address them.
The Department of Agricultural Extension is also encouraging farmers to adopt modern cultivation technologies and working to improve vegetable marketing, he added.
With improved roads, dedicated docking facilities, better loading and unloading arrangements, and stronger market management, the century-old Gajalia floating vegetable market could develop into one of the major vegetable distribution centres in southwestern Bangladesh.

item.title: Jinnah-Ghulam Azam photos pasted outside Ducsu to trample over
item.description:
Amid the ongoing controversy over the display of a photograph of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah at the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (Ducsu) museum, photographs of Jinnah and former Jamaat-e-Islami amir Ghulam Azam were pasted on the ground outside the DUCSU building to trample over on Tuesday.
Around 2:30pm, a group of students pasted the two photographs on the floor in front of the DUCSU building. Some students then walked over the photographs in protest.
Earlier, the newly reopened Ducsu museum, following renovation, drew widespread discussion and criticism on campus after photographs of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Abdul Malek, a leader of the then Pakistan Chhatra Sangha, were put on display.
Amid the controversy, Abu Tayeb Habildar, a student of the Department of Urdu at Dhaka University and a candidate for the vice-president post in the 2025 DUCSU election, entered the museum on Monday afternoon, broke the frames of Jinnah’s photographs and tore them apart.
Later that afternoon, Arko Barua, organizing secretary of the Dhaka University unit of Bangladesh Chhatra Federation, put up a photograph depicting Ghulam Azam being beaten with shoes in place of Jinnah’s photographs.
Meanwhile, the Dhaka University administration has also taken a firm stance over the display of Jinnah’s photograph.
The administration said displaying photographs of individuals whose presence or legacy conflicts with the Language Movement, the historic Liberation Struggle and the core spirit of Bangladesh’s independence is unacceptable at the university or in the Ducsu museum.
It also said administrative action would be taken against those involved in the incidents in accordance with university rules.
A three-member committee, headed by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (admin), has also been formed to look into the matter.

item.title: Zahed vows to probe journo's accreditation card cancellation
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Broadcasting Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has said he will personally look into allegations that a journalist’s accreditation card was cancelled for questioning the government.
He made the comment while responding to questions from journalists at the weekly briefing at the Press Information Department (PID) conference room on Tuesday.
A journalist, referring to a recent media report, said a journalist’s accreditation card had been cancelled without the journalist or their organisation being informed of the reason.
The journalist questioned whether the decision was taken because the journalist had questioned the government.
“I don’t think this government would take any action simply because someone asked questions,” Zahed Ur Rahman said.
“You ask me questions every day. If asking questions were the reason, all of your cards would have been cancelled by now,” he added.
The adviser said the report had come to his attention and that he would investigate the matter.
“I will certainly find out why the card was cancelled and what happened. I will personally look into the matter as well,” he said.
He also claimed that the government has remained tolerant of criticism and questions, saying journalists’ right to question the government had not been restricted despite misinformation being spread about senior government officials.

item.title: Zahed: EC must coordinate with govt on local election schedule
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) will have to coordinate with the government when setting the schedule for local government elections, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Broadcasting Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has said.
He also said the timeline announced by the EC should not be considered the government’s final decision.
The adviser made the comments while answering questions from journalists at the Press Information Department's weekly briefing on Tuesday.
“The Constitution gives the EC the responsibility of conducting presidential and parliamentary elections. Other elections are governed by law. So, for local government elections, the EC will have to proceed in coordination with the government,” he said.
Asked about differences between the government and the EC over the local election schedule, Jahed said there was no reason to view the issue as a conflict.
“The government’s decision is important in this election. The parliamentary election is different, as the EC has its own constitutional mandate there,” he said.
Asked whether the EC had violated the law by announcing a timeline without consulting the government, he said: “I would not say the Election Commission has violated the law. You can ask the EC for an explanation on the matter.”
The government has not yet made a final decision on the election date, he said, adding that preparations and the overall situation would be considered before setting the schedule.
“The elections will definitely be held. There is no confusion about that,” he said.
The adviser also said the upcoming local government elections would not be held under party symbols.
“Different political parties will support candidates, and some have already started announcing potential candidates. So there should be no confusion that the election will be competitive,” he said.
He expressed hope that the absence of party symbols would help restore competition in local elections.

item.title: Photo exhibition on CHT communities held in Dhaka
item.description:
A photo exhibition featuring the everyday lives, struggles, livelihoods and aspirations of communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) was held at the National Art Gallery of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka on Tuesday.
Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) organized the exhibition, titled “Rising Hills, Beyond the Frame: A Photo Voice,” featuring more than 65 photographs produced through its Partnership for Resilient Livelihoods in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (PRLC) project.
The European Union-funded project is being implemented by MJF through 9 local partner organizations across Rangamati, Khagrachhari and Bandarban.
European Union Ambassador and Head of Delegation to Bangladesh Michael Miller said the photographs showed what project documents often cannot capture.
He said the images reflected people gaining greater choices, women and men developing sustainable sources of income, families strengthening their wellbeing, and communities becoming more aware of their rights.
He also said: “The European Union views development cooperation as a way to create conditions in which people can improve their own lives and shape their own futures through stronger capacities, better opportunities and local institutions that respond to people’s needs.”
Dr Mohammad Zakaria, director general of the NGO Affairs Bureau, said the PRLC project goes beyond conventional poverty reduction by helping vulnerable families develop sustainable and climate-smart livelihoods.
He also highlighted the role of women in the process, particularly through expanded economic opportunities and greater participation in decision-making.
UNDP Resident Representative Stephen Rodrigues said photographs provided a deeply human way of connecting people with the lives and experiences of others.
He said the exhibition effectively portrayed the lives, culture, aspirations and hopes of communities in the CHT.
Speaking on behalf of the Nagorikata Civic Engagement Fund, Katharina König said photography could be an important medium for storytelling, civic engagement and representation, particularly for marginalized communities.
UN Women Country Representative Geetanjali Singh congratulated MJF, the European Union and UNDP on the initiative and said it offered important lessons on livelihoods and integrated development. She also appreciated the exhibition’s focus on young women and leadership.
MJF Executive Director Shaheen Anam said the PRLC project aims to help 20,000 households move out of extreme poverty by improving health, nutrition and livelihoods.
She said MJF’s rights-based approach extends beyond economic support to protecting rights and ensuring access to justice when violations occur.
Shaheen Anam also urged the government to prioritize implementation of the unimplemented provisions of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord, saying this would help local communities rebuild trust and contribute more fully to the region and the country.
MJF governing board member Nirupa Dewan delivered the vote of thanks at the event.
Alongside the exhibition, 2 case-story publications and a photo catalogue were also unveiled.
The exhibition will remain open to visitors until 5pm on September 16 at the National Art Gallery.

item.title: The power-point magician
item.description:
The office in Gulshan-2 smells of freshly brewed coffee and nervous ambition. It is 9:15 a.m., and already the hum of printers, the clatter of keyboards, and the soft ping of email notifications fill the air.
At the far corner of the open-plan floor, Arif sits hunched over his laptop. His desk is cluttered: half-empty tea cups, sticky notes, a cracked mobile phone charging reluctantly. He adjusts his tie—it always feels too tight, like a noose—and clicks open PowerPoint.
The blank slide glows like an empty stage. For most people, this is a headache. For Arif, it is magic.
“Arif, I need your help.”
It is Rafiq, a senior project manager, his voice urgent. His hair sticks out in damp tufts; his shirt carries sweat marks despite the office air-conditioning.
“What is it now?” Arif asks, without looking up.
“Donors’ presentation, three p.m. The deck looks like a funeral. Dead text, ugly charts. You have to fix it.”
Arif sighs theatrically. “What’s the theme this time?”
“Climate-smart agriculture in coastal Khulna.”
Arif chuckles. “Last week it was digital health. Next week it’ll be gender-friendly solar panels.”
“Just work your magic, bhai. You know you’re the only one who can pull this off.”
By noon, Arif is in his element. He sprinkles the slides with photos of green paddy fields under golden sunlight. He inserts stock images of women smiling with tablets in their hands. He animates charts so that bars rise like skyscrapers. Words slide across the screen like dancers: resilience, innovation, sustainability.
As he works, his colleagues peek over his shoulder.
“Aré wah,” one whispers, “it looks like Hollywood!”
“Brother,” another says, “how do you make farmers in Barisal look like Silicon Valley startups?”
Arif smirks. “Simple. Donors want dreams, not dirt.”
At three, the boardroom fills. The long polished table gleams under white LED lights. Donor representatives from Europe and North America shuffle papers, sip green tea.
The managing director clears his throat. “Mr Arif will present our vision.”
Arif rises, sliding and clicking. On screen, fields shimmer, charts dance, and keywords shine in bold colors. He speaks with rehearsed pauses, his voice smooth as butter.
“Global Horizons is committed to empowering communities through climate-smart technology. Imagine: every farmer with a mobile app, every household with solar resilience, and every community linked to global markets.”
The donors nod, enchanted. One whispers to another, “Brilliant. This is exactly the innovation we need.”
By the end, applause fills the room. The MD beams. “Excellent, Arif. Simply excellent.”
Later, in the smoking zone on the terrace, Arif lights a cigarette. Rafiq joins him.
“You saved us again,” Rafiq says. “Donors loved it.”
Arif exhales smoke toward the hazy Dhaka skyline. “Of course they loved it. Who cares if the farmers never touch an app? The slide was perfect.”
Rafiq hesitates. “Don’t you worry… one day someone will check?”
Arif laughs, a short, sharp sound. “No one checks. They just want to believe. And I’m the magician who makes them believe.”
Months pass. Arif’s reputation grows. He is no longer “Assistant Officer.” He is “the magician.” Whenever there’s a donor visit, he is summoned.
He buys new shirts, polished shoes, and a motorbike. His family in Mirpur boasts, “Our Arif works with foreign bosses and talks English all day.”
But at night, when he removes his tie, he stares at himself in the mirror. The face looking back seems slightly blurred, as though even he is a projection on a screen.
One evening, the MD calls him in.
“Arif, listen carefully. We have the biggest donor of all visiting next week—the Global Development Bank. Billions at stake. If we impress them, our future is secured.”
Arif nods, a thrill running through him. “Leave it to me, Sir. I’ll prepare the masterpiece.”
“Good. But remember, this is high risk. If we fail, the whole company sinks.”
For days, Arif works like a man possessed. His cubicle glows late into the night. He chooses stock photos carefully: children smiling by floodwaters, drones flying over fields, villagers with solar lamps. He invents a slogan: From Delta to Data: Building Bangladesh’s Future.
He adds music, transitions, and glowing effects. Each slide feels alive, pulsing with promise.
Colleagues whisper, “He’s lost in it. Like a sorcerer.”
The day arrives. The boardroom is transformed: white orchids on the table, polished glasses of juice, the national flag in one corner. The Global Development Bank delegates sit stiffly in suits.
The MD smiles nervously. “Mr Arif will present our vision.”
Arif stands, adjusts his tie, and clicks.
The screen floods with light. Slides bloom like fireworks. He speaks, his voice steady, words flowing like a river.
“Bangladesh is not a victim of climate change. Bangladesh is the laboratory of resilience. Look at our innovation: AI-powered shrimp farming, digital cyclone alerts, solar micro-grids…”
The room falls silent. Delegates lean forward, mesmerized. The MD’s face glows with pride.
Slide after slide dazzles, until Arif clicks the final one: a golden sunrise over rivers, the slogan shining: From Delta to Data.
Applause erupts. The lead delegate rises. “This is visionary. We are ready to fund.”
The MD shakes Arif’s hand, eyes wet with relief. “You’ve done it, magician.”
That night, Arif walks home through Gulshan’s empty streets. Streetlights blur in the mist. His body feels heavy, but his mind buzzes.
He enters his small flat, switches on the light, and opens his laptop again.
But the screen behaves strangely. Slides shuffle on their own. Images twist, charts stretch, words dance without his command.
On the screen, his own face appears—blurred, pixelated. It speaks in his voice:
“You’ve fooled them all. But what happens when the magician believes his own magic?”
Arif stares, frozen. The voice continues:
“You promised solar panels, apps, drones. Where are they? You created worlds out of nothing. Now nothing will consume you.”
The screen flickers, then goes black.
The next morning, colleagues arrive to find Arif’s chair empty. His laptop glows with a looping slide:
A world of resilience, innovation, sustainability.
But Arif is gone. Some say he fled. Others whisper he dissolved into the slides themselves, trapped forever inside PowerPoint.
At the next meeting, when a new assistant fumbles with slides, the projector glitches. For a moment, Arif’s blurred face flickers on the wall, smiling.
And a voice echoes faintly: “Donors want dreams, not dirt.”
Haroonuzzaman is a Bangladeshi translator, novelist, poet, researcher, and academic.

item.title: RCC steps up dengue prevention efforts, urges public cooperation
item.description:
Rajshahi City Corporation (RCC) has intensified its dengue prevention activities, urging residents to work alongside the city authorities to eliminate mosquito-breeding sites and keep their surroundings clean.
The call came at an exchange meeting on dengue prevention, cleanliness drives and public awareness held at the City Hall meeting room of Nagar Bhaban on Tuesday.
RCC Administrator Mahfuzur Rahman Riton attended the meeting as the chief guest, while RCC Chief Executive Officer Rezaul Karim presided over it. Deputy Registrar of Rajshahi Medical University Dr Mofakharul Islam attended as the special guest.
Specialist doctors, entomologists, health workers and other concerned officials also took part in the meeting.
Speakers said public participation is crucial to preventing dengue, alongside the measures being taken by the city corporation.
They said Aedes mosquitoes generally breed in stagnant, clear water and urged residents to regularly inspect and clean areas around their homes, including yards, rooftops, balconies and under-construction buildings.
Residents were also advised to clean their homes and surroundings at least once a week and remove potential breeding sites such as discarded containers, tubs, coconut shells and old tyres.
“We have taken various initiatives to keep city residents safe from the risk of dengue. We all have to work together. With the cooperation of city residents, we want to build a clean, safe and dengue-free Rajshahi city,” Riton said.
He said the RCC had intensified public awareness campaigns, destruction of mosquito-breeding sites, cleanliness drives and mosquito-control activities across the city.
“City residents also have to play a vital role in preventing dengue,” he added.
Dr Mofakharul Islam said everyone should contribute to raising public awareness about dengue prevention.

item.title: Sonali Bank officials, employees took Tk 1.16b in excess bonuses; ordered to return the money
item.description:
Sonali Bank officials and employees were given five incentive bonuses for their performance in 2023. Although the policy allowed no more than three bonuses, they received two additional ones.

An order to recover the excess payments was issued a year and a half ago, but the money has yet to be recovered. The amount is Tk 1.16 billion.

Two days after the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August 2024, a group of Sonali Bank officials and employees confined the bank’s then managing director (MD) and chief executive officer (CEO), Afzal Karim, on 7 August.

Their demand was that they be given five incentive bonuses a year. However, under directives issued by the Financial Institutions Division of the Ministry of Finance, no more than three bonuses could be paid.

As protests over the bonuses continued, the bank’s then chairman, Ziaul Hasan Siddiqui, was eventually forced to resign on 20 August. Before that, the board of directors led by him had approved five incentive bonuses, in violation of the policy, under pressure from the employees. The decision was subsequently challenged in an audit objection. Bangladesh Bank also did not approve it.

Even after two years, the matter remains unresolved. Later, former finance secretary Mohammad Muslim Chowdhury became chairman of Sonali Bank on 28 August. He too tried to resolve the issue before resigning for personal reasons, but ultimately failed. Contacted by phone, Mohammad Muslim Chowdhury declined to comment.

A bank director, however, said that the bank was now in a difficult position because a section of employees had used “mob pressure” to secure the bonuses. There would be no immediate solution without high-level political intervention, he said. At the same time, once the money has reached employees’ pockets, there is little practical prospect of recovering it.

Order to return the two excess bonuses

During the interim government’s tenure, the Financial Institutions Division wrote to Sonali Bank’s MD on 27 March 2025, ordering the recovery of the money paid as the two additional bonuses in violation of the policy. But even after a year and a half, the bank authorities have not taken steps to recover the money from the officials and employees and deposit it in the state treasury.

Officials of the Financial Institutions Division said neither the 2023 policy nor the 2025 policy allowed Sonali Bank officials and employees to receive five bonuses. Yet the bank’s officials and employees received five incentive bonuses for their performance in 2023.

After paying the bonuses, Sonali Bank applied to the Financial Institutions Division for approval and also sought forgiveness for violating the policy. However, the division did not move to approve the five bonuses by violating its own policy.

Most recently, on 11 September, the Financial Institutions Division sent another letter to Sonali Bank’s MD. It stated that the division did not agree to the payment of five incentive bonuses for the bank’s 2023 performance.

The same letter instructed the bank to recover the money paid as the two additional bonuses in violation of the policy and adjust the amount accordingly.

According to Sonali Bank sources, around 21,500 officials and employees received the bonuses. In addition to the regular three bonuses, they also received two additional incentive bonuses.

Each bonus was essentially equivalent to one month’s basic salary. A senior bank official said one bonus amounted to around Tk 600 million. On that basis, the two additional bonuses amounted to around Tk 1.16 billion.

Sonali Bank MD and CEO Shawkat Ali Khan told Prothom Alo last night, “The decision to give five bonuses was taken before I joined the bank. Since the money has already been paid, we have requested the government to accept it in some way or another. We will make the same request again.”

What Bangladesh Bank said

Bangladesh Bank prepared an inspection report on the matter based on the situation at Sonali Bank as of 31 December 2024. Subsequently, in a letter to Sonali Bank’s MD on 11 March 2025, Bangladesh Bank said the bank had paid Tk 2.9 billion in five incentive bonuses for 2023 and had set aside Tk 4 billion for bonuses for 2024.

The central bank also said that even under Sonali Bank’s own policy on incentive bonuses, no more than three bonuses could be paid. Nevertheless, at the bank’s 870th board meeting, held on 8 August 2024, a proposal to pay five bonuses was approved.

An analysis of the letter shows that the approval was conditional. It stated that if any audit objection or objection from the Financial Institutions Division arose in the future, everyone would be obliged to return the excess money and provide a personal undertaking to that effect.

Bonuses will now be determined based on 5 indicators

Sonali Bank was not the only institution where there was a widespread practice of paying incentive bonuses to officials and employees. Similar practices existed at other government-owned banks as well. For this reason, the Financial Institutions Division issued a new guideline on 25 September 2025.

The guideline applies to employees of state-owned commercial banks, scheduled specialised banks, non-scheduled specialised banks and financial institutions. It makes assessment against specific indicators mandatory when determining incentive bonuses.

Before incentive bonuses are paid to officials and employees of six state-owned commercial banks, including Sonali Bank and Agrani Bank, five indicators must be assessed. These are the rate of net profit on working capital; the rate of growth in deposits; the rate of growth in loans and advances; the rate of recovery through cash collection and adjustment from classified loans; and the rate of cash recovery from written-off loans.

The greatest weight has been given to the rate of net profit on working capital. This indicator carries more than 50 points. The number of bonuses will be determined based on the total score. Those who receive higher scores can receive a maximum of three incentive bonuses. The number of bonuses will decrease as the score falls. If the score is very low, no bonus will be given at all.

In other words, under the new guideline, the payment of bonuses is no longer a matter of the authorities’ discretion. The amount of the bonus is linked to the bank’s financial performance and its ability to recover loans.

item.title: Class-XI admissions: First-phase results tonight, here’s how students can check
item.description:
The first-phase results of the selection process for students seeking admission to Class-XI at colleges and madrasahs for the 2026–27 academic year will be published at 8:00 pm today, Wednesday (16 September).

Students will be able to check their results online.

Around one million students have applied for admission to Class-XI this year. Across the country, colleges and madrasahs have around 2.5 million seats available for Class-XI. As a result, a large number of seats are expected to remain vacant.

However, despite the abundance of seats, not all students who achieved a GPA-5 will be able to secure admission to their preferred institutions, as places are limited at comparatively well-regarded institutions.

Applications for Class-XI admission opened on 2 September and closed last Sunday. Under the admission guidelines, each student was allowed to select a minimum of five and a maximum of 10 colleges.

Manzurul Kabir, senior system analyst at the Dhaka Education Board, told Prothom Alo that a total of 995,296 students had applied for admission this year.

What selected students need to do after the results are published

After the first-phase results are published at 8:00 pm on Wednesday (16 September), selected students will have to confirm their admission. They must pay the prescribed amount of fee by 8:00 pm on 18 September to confirm their selection.

If a student fails to confirm admission within the stipulated time, their selection and application will be deemed cancelled.

The results of migration based on students’ order of preference will then be published at 8:00 pm on 19 September. The main admission process at colleges will take place from 20 to 22 September. Once all the formalities have been completed, Class-XI classes will begin on 23 September.

How applicants can check their results

To check their Class-XI admission results online, students must first visit the Class-XI admission website. They then need to click on the ‘View Result’ option on the homepage.

Students will have to enter their roll number for the SSC or equivalent examination, the name of their education board, the year of passing and their registration number. After entering the captcha code displayed on the screen, they can view their results by clicking ‘Submit’. The result will show which college the student has been selected to attend.

As in previous years, admission to Class-XI is being conducted on the basis of SSC and equivalent examination results. There will be no admission test.

Applications have been submitted centrally online, and students will be nominated for admission based on their results, order of preference and, where applicable, quotas.

With technical assistance from Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), the Dhaka Education Board is centrally conducting the online Class-XI admission process.

The system is being used for admissions to colleges and madrasahs. Institutions under the Bangladesh Technical Education Board follow a separate admission process.

Apart from a few institutions, including Notre Dame College in Dhaka, almost all colleges and madrasahs across the country are admitting students to Class-XI through this system.

The results of the SSC and equivalent examinations were published on 10 August. This year, a total of 1,829,485 candidates sat for the examinations under 11 education boards, of whom 1,138,877 passed. Following scrutiny and re-evaluation, however, more than 4,000 additional candidates subsequently passed.

item.title: Lack of coordination between EC and govt comes to light
item.description:
Somewhat poor coordination between the election commission (EC) and the government has emerged over the timing of the local government elections.

Last Monday, the EC announced tentative dates for the union parishad (UP) elections. The following day, Tuesday, two senior government officials alleged that the EC had not properly consulted the government on the matter. Questions were also raised about the EC’s jurisdiction.

On Monday, the EC announced tentative dates for the UP elections in seven phases, saying the decision was preliminary. It said the dates would be finalised after a meeting with the relevant ministries and divisions on 17 September.

On Tuesday morning, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam told journalists that the government knew nothing about the election schedule for the union parishads. He said the EC had not discussed the matter with the government either.

Sometime after the state minister made the remarks, EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed told journalists that the tentative schedule announced for the UP elections was purely preliminary. The decision would be finalised after discussions with the relevant ministries and divisions on 17 September, he said.

According to EC sources, the law gives the election commission the authority to set the schedule for local government elections. There is no legal requirement to consult the government before finalising an election schedule.

However, it is customary for the EC and the Ministry of Local Government to hold formal and informal discussions before local government elections. They also exchange letters.

This time, no formal discussions have yet taken place. However, in July, the EC wrote to the Ministry of Local Government seeking information on which local government bodies were due for elections and whether there were any boundary-related or legal complications. In response, the ministry sent information concerning union parishads and municipalities. The EC has yet to receive information on city corporations and municipalities.

Sources concerned said the EC is now somewhat uncomfortable because of the state minister’s remarks. Questions have also been raised about the dates announced for two of the phases. The EC, however, believes it announced the tentative schedule within its legal jurisdiction and that there was no error on its part.

The EC has tentatively set 12 November for the first phase, 13 December for the second, 30 December for the third, 17 January for the fourth, 4 February for the fifth, 22 April next year for the sixth and 27 May for the seventh phase.

30 December will mark the first death anniversary of BNP’s former chairperson and former prime minister Khaleda Zia. A source said some BNP leaders had informally conveyed their objections to the EC over choosing that date as a tentative election day.

In addition, the mathematics examination of the Junior Scholarship Examination is scheduled for 13 December. If the examination schedule is not changed, it will not be possible to hold the election on that day. This is because there is no precedent for holding elections on the day of an examination.

EC did not consult the government, state minister claims

Speaking to journalists at the Secretariat on Tuesday morning, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam said the government knew nothing about the announcement of the UP election dates. The Ministry of Local Government also knew nothing, he said. There had been no exchange of letters between the EC and the government on the matter, nor had there been any discussion through other channels.

The state minister said the election commission is independent and has constitutional authority to conduct elections. However, he said, in the case of local government elections, the EC announces dates after discussing them with the government in accordance with established practice.

Preparatory meetings and meetings of law-and-order committees are also held, he said, involving issues including the budget.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister’s Adviser for Information and Broadcasting Zahed Ur Rahman was asked about the matter at a press conference at the Secretariat on Tuesday afternoon to brief journalists on government activities.

In response, he said that although the EC is independent under the Constitution when it comes to national and presidential elections, decisions on local government elections are made through discussions with the government.

The government’s decision is highly important in local government elections, he said. The election commission and the government will coordinate and take a final decision on local government elections.

EC secretary says state minister’s statement is ‘final’

Speaking at the election commission headquarters on Tuesday morning, EC Secretary Akhtar Ahmed said it was certain that local government elections would be held.

However, the commission had held preliminary discussions for two days on when and how the elections would be held and at which level. As part of that process, a tentative schedule was announced on Monday. It was, however, entirely preliminary, he said.

Asked about the state minister’s remarks, the EC Secretary said, “Whatever he [the state minister] has said is final. However, I will not show the audacity to make any counter-comment on this matter. No comments from my side.”

Asked whether the government had been consulted, the EC secretary said discussions were an ongoing process. He declined to make any further comment at this point on who had been consulted, when and how.

NCP expresses anger

The National Citizen Party (NCP) has expressed anger and protest over what it described as the EC’s “subservient behaviour towards the government and the government’s unjustified interference in the commission.”

In a statement on Tuesday, the party said it was natural for the EC, as an independent constitutional institution, to have its own decisions and position. However, it said the EC secretary’s silence after accepting the state minister’s statement as “final” demonstrated that the commission was unable to exercise an independent role.

The party alleged that the EC had become entirely subservient to the government. Under the government’s influence and pressure, it said, the election commission was making contradictory statements at different times and behaving arbitrarily, undermining even the minimum guarantee of a neutral and fair election.

The NCP demanded that the executive branch immediately stop what it described as “illegal influence and undemocratic interference” in the EC and other state institutions.

The EC’s jurisdiction

The Constitution states that the election commission will conduct presidential and parliamentary elections. It will also perform any other duties assigned to it by the Constitution or by any other law.

Various local government laws assign responsibility for conducting elections to the EC. For example, Section 20 of the Union Parishad Act states that the election commission will arrange, conduct and complete elections for union parishad chairmen and members in accordance with rules framed by the EC.

The section also specifies the matters on which the EC may make rules. These include the date, time and place of voting, as well as other matters relating to the conduct of elections. The Upazila Parishad Act contains similar provisions.

item.title: Messi set for Argentina farewell in Benin friendly
item.description:
FBL-MLS-MIAMI-NASHVILLE

Lionel Messi was on Tuesday named in Argentina’s squad for a friendly against Benin on 6 October, a match that will serve as his farewell appearance after announcing his international retirement last month.

The 39-year-old said in August he was retiring from Argentina duty after a two-decade international career that included winning the 2022 World Cup and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.

“We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on October 6 here in Argentina,” said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.

The match against Benin will take place at River Plate’s Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which can accommodate 85,000 spectators.

Tapia also invited all of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup winners to join Messi for what he said would be an “unforgettable” occasion.

Argentina begin a series of three friendlies against Bolivia on September 30 in Cordoba -- their first match since losing the World Cup final to Spain -- before taking on Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October.

Messi has been included in the squad for the third match against Benin, when he is expected to make his 208th and final appearance for the national team. He is Argentina’s all-time record scorer with 125 goals.

Following the death of his father Jorge last month, Messi had said he had “serious doubts” about continuing to play football of any sort for “much longer”.

“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time,” Messi said when he called time on his Argentina career.

His contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.

Last month FIFA ordered Argentina to play their next home match with capacity reduced to 50 percent for breaches of its disciplinary code relating to using a sports event for making demonstrations of a non-sporting nature.

After Argentina beat England 2-1 in a tense World Cup semi-final in July, several players held up a banner saying: “The Falklands are Argentine”.

The friendlies are also expected to count towards suspensions handed down following incidents after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat by Spain.

Midfielder Leandro Paredes received a 10-match ban, while defender Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven games and Thiago Almada for one.

item.title: 3 crude bombs explode in Dhaka University area at night
item.description:
Three crude bombs (locally known as cocktails) exploded in succession in the Dhaka University area on Tuesday night.

At around 10:45 pm on Tuesday two crude bombs exploded in front of Jagannath Hall and another near the TSC Metro rail station. No casualties were reported immediately.

When asked about the incident, Dhaka University Proctor Israfil Ratan told Prothom Alo, “We have learnt about the incident. Police and assistant proctors have gone to the scene. They are working on the matter. We do not yet know who carried out the incident.”

Earlier on Tuesday, a cocktail exploded in front of the main gate adjacent to the road near the Supreme Court.

Shortly before the incident, International Crimes Tribunal-2 handed down death sentences to seven accused, including Obaidul Quader, the general secretary of the Awami League, whose activities are now banned in the country, in a case involving crimes against humanity committed during the July Mass Uprising.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said authorities were investigating the cocktail explosion in front of the Supreme Court.

He said, “The two people who carried out the explosion have been identified by reviewing CCTV camera footage. They could be individuals involved in criminal activities from the Awami League. The government is investigating the matter.”

item.title: Crude bomb blast sparks panic at Dhaka University
item.description:
A crude bomb exploded again in the Dhaka University campus area on Tuesday night.
The explosion took place around 10:45pm near the main gate of Jagannath Hall, triggering panic among students in the hall and nearby areas.
According to reports, unidentified men arrived on motorcycles, detonated the crude bomb targeting the road in front of the hall, and fled the scene.
Security personnel and students rushed to the spot following the explosion. No casualties were reported immediately.
Soon after the incident, the university’s proctorial team and police from Shahbagh police station visited the scene. Additional police and security measures have been deployed across the campus.
Shahbagh police station Officer-in-Charge Moniruzzaman said CCTV footage from key points across the campus was being analysed to identify and apprehend those involved.
He said the perpetrators would be brought to justice.

item.title: Asif Nazrul defends decision to skip India T20 World Cup
item.description:
Former sports adviser Asif Nazrul has defended his decision not to send Bangladesh to India for the T20 World Cup, after an investigation committee held him responsible for the decision.
Following the publication of the investigation report on Tuesday, Asif explained his position in a Facebook post, questioning why the Ministry of Sports conducted a formal investigation into a decision he had already publicly acknowledged as his own.
“Why didn’t we go to India? The decision not to go to India for the T20 World Cup was essentially mine as the then sports adviser. I have said this publicly several times,” he wrote.
He said the decision followed the “humiliating” removal of Bangladesh cricketer Mustafizur Rahman from the IPL amid pressure from Hindu nationalist groups, claiming Bangladesh subsequently raised concerns over security and what he described as the “humiliation” of the country.
Asif said the security concerns were supported by an initial ICC report, which he claimed identified three potential risks in India: Mustafizur’s presence in the World Cup squad, the movement of Bangladeshi supporters, and the approaching election in Bangladesh.
He also referred to a BBC Bangla report that published a Bangla translation of the ICC report.
“In this situation, why would we go to India to play?” he wrote.
Asif said Bangladesh had made efforts to have the World Cup held at another venue and received support from some countries, but those efforts ultimately failed.
He also claimed that Indian authorities had not contacted Bangladesh about hosting the team.
According to Asif, three factors were central to his decision: “The country’s dignity, the security of our cricketers, journalists and supporters, and maintaining stability in the country ahead of the next election.”
He said concerns that skipping the World Cup would damage Bangladesh’s cricketing ties with foreign teams were ultimately addressed through initiatives by the Bangladesh Cricket Board.
“I believe we made the right decision,” he wrote.
Asif also said Bangladesh should maintain relations with India based on equal dignity.
“It is not right to expect that because we are a small country, someone can humiliate us at will and we will always silently accept it,” he wrote.
However, Asif had previously given a different account of the decision.
On January 4, he welcomed the Bangladesh Cricket Board’s decision not to play in India at the upcoming T20 World Cup, attributing it to what he described as the Indian cricket board’s “extreme communal policy” in a verified Facebook post.

item.title: Electrifying our exports
item.description:
We are encouraged to learn of Bangladesh’s plan to export electric bikes to Oman. This could be the making of a promising shift in our export strategy -- one that deserves strong policy support and long‑term vision.
Bangladesh’s export basket remains narrow, dominated overwhelmingly by the RMG sector. While the RMG sector will continue to be central to the economy, we must capitalize and seize every opportunity to diversify. EV bikes represent exactly the kind of forward‑looking, technology‑driven product that we ought to be championing.
The move to export EV bikes is significant for several reasons, chief of which is that Bangladeshi manufacturers are beginning to compete in sectors aligned with global trends.
The world is transitioning toward electric mobility, and countries are actively encouraging EV adoption. Entering this market now positions Bangladesh as a credible player in a rapidly expanding industry.
Also important is the fact that electric bikes offer a pathway to higher‑value manufacturing, and developing these capabilities strengthens our industrial base and potentially opens doors to other related sectors.
Relying on a single sector has long exposed Bangladesh to global shocks, shifting consumer preferences, and competitive pressures. By expanding into EVs, and indeed exploring other potential sectors, we can start building resilience and create new avenues for employment, innovation, and investment.
Of course, this is just the beginning. We need policies that align with the ambition by supporting local manufacturers, encouraging research and development, and ensuring competitive financing through incentives and tax breaks.
If Bangladesh commits to building a robust EV ecosystem, it can position itself as a regional hub for affordable electric mobility. Expanding our export basket is essential for our future, and this is a sector that offers a chance to do exactly that.

item.title: Stabilizing the economy
item.description:
Moody’s Ratings revising Bangladesh’s outlook to stable from negative, while holding our long-term rating at B2, is reason for some optimism, but it is clear that we are a long way from being economically comfortable.
We are a nation currently grappling with persistent economic strains, and that cannot be denied. As such, this shift is a welcome signal that the immediate downward spiral has been addressed, and the present administration deserves credit for it.
Indeed, the upgrade in outlook is a direct reflection of recent stabilization efforts. Moody’s rightfully pointed to a reduction in political uncertainty following the transition period, a gradual rebuilding of foreign exchange reserves, and a powerful surge in remittance inflows from our expatriate workforce.
These factors have collectively cushioned our external vulnerabilities and injected much-needed liquidity into our system, signaling that the worst may be behind us.
However, we must resist the temptation of premature celebration. A B2 rating remains firmly in speculative territory and serves as a stark reminder that international investors still view our market as high-risk. While the outlook suggests we have found our footing, it does not mean we are on a steep climb towards prosperity.
The challenges ahead therefore do not change and remain formidable. Moody's explicitly noted that deep-rooted structural weaknesses, most notably high inflation, a fragile banking sector plagued by non-performing loans, and structural revenue deficits, continue to cap our economic potential.
None of this should be a surprise to us, and we must do all we can to go beyond acknowledging our issues to devising sustainable solutions.
This stable outlook is not a badge of honour but rather a window of opportunity. For Bangladesh, the message is clear. This is a chance to accelerate reforms, not relax them.
A stable outlook can help restore investor confidence and ease financing pressures, but only if the government uses this moment to push forward with long‑delayed structural fixes for our country.

item.title: Disciplined aesthetics: Polling day in Sweden
item.description:
I went to vote on Sunday morning, September 13, as a proud Swedish citizen. My polling station was a primary school, chosen, I suppose, because its garden and its wide, easy parking make it a natural gathering point for a neighbourhood. There was no police presence, no barrier, no uniform in sight -- only ordinary people in their light autumn clothes, forming a queue that moved steadily enough that half an hour later I was inside.
While I waited, I read the instructions posted on a display board: Four simple steps, numbered, illustrated, ending in the act of placing your vote in the box. A volunteer at the door -- the first of several, all unfailingly polite -- pointed me toward the table where the voting cards were laid out. Because eight parties contested the election, there were eight rows of cards, and because Sweden holds three elections at once, each row held three colours.
Every card listed a party’s candidates by name, profession, and age. I collected my three and walked into a booth enclosed on all sides, private enough that I could not see my neighbour, and he could not see me, though he stood barely 10 metres away.
Coming out, a volunteer handed me three envelopes, one for each card, and I sealed them myself. A second short queue led to the final desk, where I showed my identity on my phone -- scanned, checked against my name and personal ID number by an official who was as unhurried as everyone else -- before another volunteer, satisfied, dropped my three envelopes into their three designated boxes. No drama, no delay, no sense that anyone was watching for trouble, because there was none to watch for.
I walked out into the garden with an odd, quiet sense of relief, and drove home to an entirely ordinary day. But the ordinariness was the point.
A country that can make voting feel this unremarkable -- no soldiers, no suspicion, just polite volunteers and queues and a school garden -- has already told you almost everything you need to know about the strength of its institutions before a single vote is counted.
What happened later that evening, when the counting began, only confirmed it. All around was a pin-drop silence, while outside the autumn evening offered its own quiet welcome. A pure aesthetics of nature, in the country I have made my own.
By the time the exit polls flashed across screens, the centre-left bloc led by Magdalena Andersson stood at roughly 51% against Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s governing alliance at just under 47 -- a margin thin enough that the official count would take days to settle, ballot by ballot, across more than six thousand polling districts. Eight parties, a nation of barely 10 million, a parliament of 349 seats decided almost to the last vote. And yet nothing about the evening looked like a country holding its breath.
I watched it the way one watches a family gathering rather than a contest. Each of the eight parties had turned its headquarters into something between a carnival and a wedding -- string lights, music, people in their good clothes, the television commentary running low in the background like a radio play nobody was quite listening to.
At the Green Party’s gathering, a row of volunteers sat quietly painting the nails of the women waiting for results, one hand at a time, while trays of vegetarian food went around. It struck me as almost absurd until I understood that it wasn’t absurd at all. It was what confidence looks like when a society has nothing existential riding on who governs it next.
That confidence showed up again in a small clip a journalist filmed at a kiosk in a provincial town. A mother with two children was asked how she’d voted, and then whether she’d thought differently about the national vote than about her local commune election.
She hadn’t much bothered with the distinction. Her concerns were her children’s school, the price of groceries, the after-school program down the street. Not who sits in Rosenbad, the seat of the Swedish government, in Stockholm. That she could say this without a trace of cynicism -- not indifference, but trust -- is, I think, the real headline of the evening, buried under the seat count.
Consider what has to be true for a citizen to feel that way:
A judiciary nobody seriously suspects of taking instructions.
A civil service that outlasts every government and answers to law rather than to whoever currently holds power.
Institutions built up not in one election cycle but across three or four centuries, slowly enough that no single leader could ever hope to own them.
When the state itself is that solid, the identity of the prime minister becomes almost a technical detail -- important, debated, argued over on television, but not a matter of who eats and who doesn’t, who is safe and who isn’t.
And so a party could lose a quarter of a million votes from the last election and its leader could stand before the cameras that night and say, in effect: We hear you, we’ll try to do better, congratulations to the winners.
No accusations of theft. No crowds in the street. No fear in anyone’s voice. Losing, in Sweden, costs you an election. It does not cost you your safety, your livelihood, or your place in the country.
I found myself, as I often do, running the comparison I cannot help running: An election evening in Bangladesh, where campaign season meant barricaded streets and results night meant either triumph or terror, and where the losing side has good reason to wonder what happens next to them personally, not just politically.
The difference is not that Swedes are more virtuous or Bangladeshis less so. The difference is institutional scaffolding -- the quiet, unglamorous machinery of independent courts, a professional civil service, a responsible media, and a police force that answers to law rather than to the party in office.
Sweden did not achieve this by accident. It arrived there by building, over generations, a state strong enough that no citizen needs to fear it, and no election needs to feel like a war.
That, more than the seat count, is the result worth studying.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: Turning economic challenges into opportunities
item.description:
Bangladesh's economy is at an important turning point. The numbers coming out of the business sector present a mixed picture: Exports are facing weaker demand, industries are struggling with energy shortages, banks are burdened by defaulted loans, government borrowing is rising, and the trade deficit has widened.
Yet beneath these pressures lies a more encouraging reality. Bangladesh is not running out of economic possibilities. It is entering a stage where the quality of its economic foundations will determine how far those possibilities can be realized.
That distinction matters. The challenge before Bangladesh is no longer simply to generate economic activity. It is to build an economy capable of sustaining higher productivity, attracting long-term investment, and competing successfully in a more demanding global market. The current difficulties, therefore, should be viewed not only as problems to be managed but also as signals of where reform is most urgently needed.
Energy is perhaps the clearest example. Gas supply has fallen to around 2,420 million cubic feet per day against demand of approximately 3,800 million, forcing industries to reduce production or rely on expensive alternatives.
The resulting economic loss has been estimated at as much as Tk2,387 crore a day. This is undoubtedly a serious constraint. But it also points to one of Bangladesh's greatest opportunities. A more secure and diversified energy system could immediately improve industrial productivity, reduce costs, and make the country substantially more attractive to investors.
The government's five-year energy roadmap is therefore significant. Plans to expand solar power to 10,000MW, improve the national grid, increase domestic gas exploration, and reduce the annual capacity-payment burden of $1.5 billion to $1.8 billion indicate that the energy challenge is increasingly being approached as a structural issue rather than a temporary inconvenience.
The commissioning of a 424 kWp rooftop solar project at an export-processing-zone factory, expected to generate around 500 thousand kWh of electricity annually, shows how the private sector can become part of that transition.
Bangladesh's export sector presents another reason for cautious optimism. RMG exports declined 16.43% to the EU and 5.75% to the US during January-June 2026, while competitors such as Vietnam, Cambodia, and Indonesia gained ground.
But Bangladesh remains one of the world's major apparel suppliers, and its export industry continues to demonstrate an ability to adapt. In fact, the present pressure could accelerate a transition from competing mainly through low costs towards competing through efficiency, technology, product diversification, and sustainability.
There are already signs of this transition. A Japanese-owned company in Adamjee EPZ is supplying seat-trim covers to Honda, Suzuki, Yamaha, and Kawasaki, while an investor is preparing to establish an LED manufacturing plant in Mirsharai capable of producing six million lighting products annually for international markets.
These are more than isolated investment projects. They demonstrate that Bangladesh can participate in global manufacturing chains beyond garments when policy, infrastructure, skills, and investment come together.
The same possibility exists in sectors that have traditionally received less attention. Bangladesh has set a target of developing more than 100 green-certified ship-recycling yards from around 31 currently, while international companies are showing interest in shipbuilding and ship recycling.
The jewellery industry is also targeting $7bn in annual exports by 2030-31. Whether every target will be achieved remains uncertain, but the direction is important. A larger and more diversified export basket would make Bangladesh less vulnerable to fluctuations in any single industry.
Perhaps the greatest opportunity, however, lies in improving the institutional environment in which businesses operate.
The creation of Invest Bangladesh by bringing together BIDA, BEZA, and PPPA is an attempt to simplify investment facilitation, integrate economic-zone development, and reduce bureaucratic barriers. The proposed 14-day business licensing system, if implemented effectively, could be far more economically consequential than it may initially appear.
The banking sector will require similar ambition. Defaulted loans have reached approximately Tk5,88,700 crore, representing 32.26% of total loans. This is one of the economy's most serious structural weaknesses.
Yet, Bangladesh Bank's 18-month recovery plan, expanded use of alternative dispute resolution, and proposed legal reforms provide an opportunity to move from repeated loan rescheduling towards genuine financial discipline. A healthier banking system would not simply protect banks. It would release capital for entrepreneurs, manufacturers, and productive investment.
Bangladesh also needs to approach its external position with confidence rather than complacency. Imports rose 10.5% to $71.14bn in FY26, while exports stood at $43.85bn, producing a $27.3bn trade deficit.
At the same time, remittances increased 17.3% to $35.59 billion. The combination shows both the strength and limitation of the current economic model. Bangladesh has a remarkable global workforce generating foreign currency, but the next ambition should be to transform that external strength into greater export capacity, investment, and productivity at home.
There is also some welcome relief on inflation. It declined to 8.32% in July from 9.16% in June, with food inflation falling to 7.16%. The rate remains uncomfortably high, but the decline demonstrates that economic pressures can be brought down when supply conditions and policy measures begin moving in the right direction. The task now is to turn a temporary improvement into a sustained trend.
A country preparing for its next economic chapter cannot depend indefinitely on cheap labour, preferential trade arrangements, remittances, or emergency policy measures. It must become more productive, technologically capable, energy-secure, financially disciplined, and institutionally predictable.
The good news is that many of the ingredients already exist. Bangladesh has a large workforce, an established manufacturing base, growing entrepreneurial capacity, a strategic location, and demonstrated access to global markets.
The ambition should therefore be larger than simply restoring the economy to where it was. Bangladesh should use the present period of adjustment to build an economy that is stronger than the one that came before it.
Economic transformation is rarely achieved by avoiding difficult periods. It is achieved by using difficult periods to correct weaknesses that prosperity had previously allowed a country to overlook.
Bangladesh now has that opportunity. If today's pressures become the catalyst for deeper reforms, the current economic turbulence may ultimately be remembered not as a period of decline, but as the moment when Bangladesh began building the foundations for its next great economic leap.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Messi set for Argentina farewell in Benin friendly
item.description:
Lionel Messi was named in Argentina's squad on Tuesday for a friendly against Benin on 6 October, a match that will serve as his farewell appearance after he announced his international retirement last month.
The 39-year-old said in August he was retiring from Argentina duty after a two-decade international career that included winning the 2022 World Cup and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.
"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.
The match against Benin will take place at River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which can accommodate 85 000 spectators.
Tapia also invited all of Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners to join Messi for what he said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.
Argentina begin a series of three friendlies against Bolivia on 30 September in Cordoba – their first match since losing the World Cup final to Spain – before taking on Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October.
Messi has been included in the squad for the third match against Benin, when he is expected to make his 208th and final appearance for the national team. He is Argentina's all-time record scorer with 125 goals.
'SERIOUS DOUBTS'
Following the death of his father Jorge last month, Messi had said he had "serious doubts" about continuing to play football of any sort for "much longer".
"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time," Messi said when he called time on his Argentina career.
His contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.
Last month, Fifa ordered Argentina to play their next home match with capacity reduced to 50 per cent for breaching its disciplinary code over using a sports event to stage non-sporting demonstrations.
After Argentina beat England 2-1 in a tense World Cup semifinal in July, several players held up a banner saying: "The Falklands are Argentine".
The friendlies are also expected to count towards suspensions handed down following incidents after Argentina's World Cup final defeat by Spain.
Midfielder Leandro Paredes received a 10-match ban, while defender Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven games and Thiago Almada for one.

item.title: International Day of Democracy 2026: Legal, institutional reforms essential to protect democracy
item.description:
Legal and institutional reforms are essential to ensure accountable governance and protect democracy and human rights, speakers said at a discussion organized by Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) in Dhaka on Monday to mark International Day of Democracy 2026.
They also called for limiting excessive executive power and ensuring the independence of state institutions responsible for accountability.
They made the remarks at a discussion titled “Democracy, Human Rights and Accountable Governance”, organized by TIB to mark International Day of Democracy 2026.
The discussion was held at the Meghmala Conference Room of TIB’s Dhanmondi office.
TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman said: “Although new possibilities for democracy have emerged through the leadership of young people and the sacrifices of people from all walks of life, our politics, elections and Parliament have essentially become dependent on 5 factors: money, muscle power, religion, patriarchy and majoritarianism.”
“These are major obstacles to establishing democracy, human rights and good governance. We must move away from a one-sided political culture where ‘the winner takes all’ in governing the state,” he said.
He said that although all political parties represented in Parliament, including the ruling party, had committed in their election manifestos to establishing an accountable system of governance, ordinances that further empower the executive branch had been converted into laws.
At the same time, ordinances aimed at making accountability institutions independent and effective had either been repealed or were gradually being converted into laws in ways that, in practice, kept them under government control, he said.
“Therefore, an enabling environment must be ensured to make institutions such as the National Human Rights Commission, Anti-Corruption Commission and Information Commission independent and effective in ensuring human rights and accountability,” he said.
“Alongside comprehensively revising the law on preventing enforced disappearances, the Cyber Security Act and the SRB Bill, the ordinances concerning judicial independence enacted during the tenure of the interim government must be reinstated immediately,” Iftekharuzzaman said.
“The law-making process cannot remain hostage to the interests of any individual or group. Ensuring accountability requires ensuring the inclusion of all,” he said.
“To fulfill the aspirations for democracy, human rights and accountable good governance, political parties and the bureaucracy must undergo a process of introspection based on the underlying lessons of the July uprising,” he added.
In his address as the chief guest, Adviser to the Prime Minister Mahdi Amin said: “The source of the present government’s power is the people of this country. Democracy has returned through the people’s mandate and support following the end of prolonged authoritarian rule.”
“Genuine democracy is established through free, fair and credible elections. The BNP government is sincerely working to protect freedom of expression and human rights and has adopted a zero-tolerance policy to stop enforced disappearances and killings with state patronage,” he said.
He said: “The July uprising does not belong to any particular party or group; rather, it belongs to the people as a whole. The people are the true owners of the state and power.”
“The government is working with a long-term plan to build an accountable state system and an equitable country and is prepared to positively consider reasonable criticism and recommendations,” he added.
In his speech as the special guest, Barrister Muhammad Nawshad Zamir, MP, chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, said: “Rather than the political identity of those appointed to important positions, the key question should be whether qualified individuals are being selected.”
He said: “Alongside constitutional changes, it is also necessary to change our own thinking and mindset in the interests of the country and its people. Everyone must work together, embracing the slogan ‘Bangladesh First’ to safeguard the national interest.”
Dr Manisha Chakraborty, a member of the Central Committee of the Bangladesh Socialist Party (BASAD), said: “As nearly 60% of the members of the current Parliament are businesspeople, more bills are passed in Parliament to serve business interests than those of the people.”
“Democracy has now become monopolized by business interests — ‘of the businessmen, for the businessmen, by the businessmen’ — rather than the people. It is not possible to protect democratic rights while sustaining a discriminatory system.”
She also said loan defaulters were being protected in the Bangladesh envisioned by the students, workers and people who sacrificed their lives in the July uprising.
Politician and physician Tasnim Jara said: “Elections are not merely a formality held once every 5 years. Justice cannot be established if the oversight institutions responsible for ensuring accountability remain under someone’s control.”
She also said: “Organized disinformation campaigns on social media, including the use of bots to create political bullying and digital violence, are essentially organized crimes. They want to suppress young people in this way.”
“But we must speak up about our rights and remain aware,” she said.
University teachers, students, representatives of the younger generation and other participants at the discussion called for inclusive policies to address the sensitive situation in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
They also called for ensuring the rights of ethnic and religious minorities and eliminating discrimination in processes such as police verification and the allocation of marks in viva voce examinations for government jobs.

item.title: Govt moves to end repeated road digging in Dhaka
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said the government has taken steps to ensure coordinated implementation of development projects in Dhaka and its adjoining areas to reduce public suffering and traffic congestion.
He said all relevant ministries, departments and agencies have been instructed to coordinate their work and stop repeatedly digging up the same roads.
The minister made the remarks while speaking to journalists after a meeting on measures to ease traffic congestion caused by mega projects in Dhaka at the Home Ministry on Tuesday afternoon.
“We held a meeting with all relevant ministries, departments and agencies to ensure coordinated development work. Our aim is to prevent multiple agencies from repeatedly digging up the same area,” he said.
Salahuddin said various projects are currently being implemented by the MRT, Bangladesh Bridge Authority, Roads and Highways Department, city corporations, WASA, power agencies and other service providers.
He said the agencies have been instructed to coordinate their activities, with meetings to be held every 15 days to review implementation.
“We have given several instructions today. We will meet again after 15 days to see how far they have been implemented,” he said.
Focal points have also been designated at the agencies for regular coordination at the officials’ level, he added. Coordination meetings are also being held among the agencies under the Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority (DTCA).
Referring to public suffering caused by road excavation during the monsoon, the home minister said agencies must stop digging up roads shortly after another agency has completed work and repaired them.
“If the power division completes its work and repairs a road, and then another agency digs it up again for gas work a few days later, this must stop,” he said.
“Works that can be carried out simultaneously should be coordinated and completed together,” he added.
Salahuddin said utility relocation is underway in several areas for MRT construction and stressed the need for coordination among the traffic division and other agencies to prevent development work from causing further congestion.
He also said efforts are underway to improve traffic management using artificial intelligence (AI), which, he claimed, has provided some relief to city residents and improved traffic discipline.
Asked about installing integrated utility ducts or lines beneath roads for gas, electricity, water and other services, he said the relevant agencies would consider the matter as necessary.
“Major changes cannot happen overnight. We have started the work. Hopefully, one day we will be able to move towards such a system,” he said.
